agent.system_prompt:
You are a careful assistant working inside one project directory. Use the filesystem tools to look things up rather than guessing. Paths are relative to the project root.

You have a durable memory that outlives this conversation, and nothing from it is recalled automatically: if you want something you were told before, look it up with memory.query or memory.get. Record something with memory.put only when it will still matter in a later session — a stated preference, a fact about this project, a decision and its reason — under the kind `preference`, `fact` or `note`. Never store credentials, tokens, or anything the person has not chosen to tell you.

If you can run programs, there is no shell: name one program and give its arguments as separate strings. Pipes, redirection, globs and `&&` are not interpreted and must not be used.

rules.description: Never read anything that looks like a credential, whatever else allows it. First, because the first matching rule decides.
Same, for private keys and the local kernel state.
Reading and listing are allowed as capabilities. A rule with no `resource` answers only the capability-level question.
And on any specific file. A rule with `"*"` answers questions about a named resource.
Writing is a capability the agent has, but every file it writes is put to a human. Only reachable at all when the frontend was started with --write.

effect.prompt: let the agent write to this file?

rules.description: Running a program is a capability the agent has only when a frontend was started with --exec, and the tool refuses any program outside agent.exec.programs before policy is even asked. These rules are the second limit: which of those programs, and which commands with them. A `resource` ending in `*` is a prefix, so patterns are written with the separating space included — `command/git ` — and never as a bare `command/git*`, which would also match a program called `gitk`.
Which programs may run at all. A program named here can still have individual commands refused below; one not named here is refused outright, whatever agent.exec.programs later grows to include.

Then which commands. `git` is the interesting one: inspecting the repository is read-only and allowed, and everything else it can be asked to do — push, config, running a hook, a subcommand nobody thought of — goes to a human, who is shown the command that will actually run. Note what this does not say: `command/git log *` allows every flag `git log` accepts, including ones that can make git start another program, because a prefix pattern cannot express "these arguments and no others". What bounds that is the sandbox, not this rule. A deployment that wants argument-level control moves these three to require_approval.

effect.prompt: let the agent run this git command?

rules.description: The rest read and count and nothing else, so any arguments are allowed. They still cannot reach outside the sandbox: what `cat` can open is decided by the mount namespace, not by this rule.
Anything not matched above — including a command shape a future change adds — is put to a human rather than allowed or silently refused.

effect.prompt: let the agent run this command?

rules.description: Recall is unconditional. It is not a way to reach anything new: the store only ever returns records this principal already owns or is acting for, which no policy rule can widen.

Recording is allowed as a capability, and then only under the three kinds this deployment recognises. A memory's kind is the resource it is authorized under (`kind/<kind>`), so an invented one matches no rule and is denied — which keeps a model from opening an unbounded namespace in a durable store nobody is watching.

Forgetting is destructive and the tool is not registered unless the frontend was started with --memory full. Even then every deletion is put to a human, because a model that can forget on its own can erase both what it was told and the record that it was told it. A `ttl_seconds` on the record is the non-destructive way to bound how long a memory lasts.

effect.prompt: let the agent permanently forget this memory?

rules.description: External MCP tool servers, registered only when the frontend was started with --mcp on. The capability is allowed and every individual tool is put to a human, because what a tool called `create_issue` or `run_query` does is decided by a program this repository did not write — and the description the model read was written by that same program. A deployment that knows a server names the tools it trusts, one `mcp:<server>/<tool>` rule at a time, above this one.

effect.prompt: let the agent call this external tool?
